# MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization

Yunhui Jang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work done during an internship at Genentech
\$ˆ†\$ Correspondence Affiliation:  KAIST    Zach Wang Affiliation: 
KAIST    Jai Doshi Affiliation:  Genentech yunhuijang@kaist.ac.kr,
{lisanza.sidney, joren.taylor}@gene.com    Kangway Chauang Affiliation:

###### Abstract

Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and
retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions.
Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language
and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is
narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization,
experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific
context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should
be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how
interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for
biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and
structured, and we introduce MemIG. This memory construction framework
realizes these three properties. In detail, MemIG addresses each insight
with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative
effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and
retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MemIG connects insights whose
interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by
decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MemIG improves
performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization
tasks.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents can self-evolve by accumulating memories from previous
rollouts, which guide future decisions ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib29)). This offers a
practical, economical alternative to fine-tuning, as the agent improves
without expensive training while accumulated memory remains
interpretable and editable. Nevertheless, the representation of this
memory is free-form and unstructured, with experience from previous
rollouts stored in natural language. This fits tasks whose experience is
narratable, such as question answering and long-horizon
conversation ([Zhong et al., 2024](#bib.bib32); [Packer et al.,
2023](#bib.bib20); [Chhikara et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), where experience
can be summarized in a sentence without losing rich information.

However, directly applying such narrative memory systems to biomolecule
optimization is not straightforward. For instance, in a computational
oracle-guided protein optimization task ([Notin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17); [Stanton et al., 2022](#bib.bib23); [Gruver et al.,
2023](#bib.bib10)), an agent proposes mutations to sequences, evaluates
the candidate using oracles, and reuses measurements from the candidates
to guide later proposals. Each evaluation is not merely a narratable
experience, but a numerical measurement tied to a specific biological
context, whose effect may depend on other co-applied mutations.
Therefore, memory for biomolecule optimization should be _indexable_ by
biological context, _quantitative_ in what it stores, and _structured_
to capture interactions between mutations.

First, memory should be indexed by the context in which a measurement
applies. Without such an index, there is no way to address a single
entry, so incorporating a new experience requires an LLM to rewrite or
summarize the entire memory. To address this, recent work ([Zhang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib29); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)) introduces
identifiers for each memory entry so that updates can be applied
locally, but these identifiers are arbitrary labels without information
about the context, so retrieval still relies on textual similarity. In
contrast, the effect of the same mutation can depend on its exact
biological context ([Notin et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Olsen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)). Therefore, memory should address each entry by this
context, so that updates and retrieval operate over the context rather
than textual similarity.

Second, memory should preserve quantitative measurements rather than
store them as free-form text. Existing memory methods store experience
as natural language authored by an LLM ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib31);
[Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), where a reported number is written
rather than computed and is therefore not tied to the measurement that
produced it. This can discard the quantitative signal required for
scientific optimization. Memory should instead retain oracle outputs as
persistent quantitative records, while the LLM only converts the
retrieved records into interpretable guidance for the agent.

Third, memory should capture the measured dependence between entities,
rather than semantic similarity between the textual records. Graph-based
memories organize records as linked notes rather than a flat list, but
their edges represent semantic relatedness between texts ([Chhikara
et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)). However, in
biomolecule optimization, the effect of one mutation can depend on the
presence of another, a phenomenon known as epistasis. Memory should
therefore record these interactions explicitly rather than assume that
mutation effects are additive.

Figure 1: Overview of MemIG. MemIG constructs an epistasis graph with
antibody-grounded identifiers. Directed edges organize property
$`\rightarrow`$ germline $`\rightarrow`$ region $`\rightarrow`$ mutation
hierarchies, while undirected edges connect co-occurring mutations and
store their epistatic effects.

To address this, we introduce MemIG (Memory as Indexable Graphs), a
domain-grounded memory construction framework for protein optimization
agents, as described in
 [Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
We focus on the domain of antibody optimization and design. To make
memory indexable, we define an antibody-grounded identifier that
specifies the target property, the germline gene, the antibody region,
and the AHo-numbered ([Honegger & PluÈckthun, 2001](#bib.bib11))
mutation, so that each record is addressed by the biological context in
which it applies. To make memory quantitative, each insight stores the
effect computed by the oracle.

Moreover, to build structured memory, MemIG creates a graph of
co-occurring insights. Here, each edge in the graph connects mutations
showing epistasis, quantified as the deviation of the joint effect from
the sum of the individual effects. Next, before each rollout, MemIG
retrieves insights from the graph based on the context identifier, ranks
them by their measured effects, and provides the selected insights with
their graph neighborhoods to the agent. Then an LLM renders them as
interpretable guidance while the quantitative memory remains. We
empirically showed that incorporating MemIG into frontier
LLMs ([GLM-5-Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Anthropic,
2025](#bib.bib2)) improves performance in the majority of settings in in
silico antibody optimization tasks.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We introduce MemIG, an _indexable_, _quantitative_, and _structured_
  memory system which addresses each insight with an antibody-grounded
  identifier and stores the effect computed by a property oracle, so
  that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup.
- •
  We construct a graph-based memory over insights, where an edge stores
  the epistatic effect of mutations, so that memory precisely records
  how mutations combine.
- •
  We demonstrate that MemIG outperforms existing memory systems on
  antibody optimization.

## 2 Method: MemIG

![Refer to caption](2610.41245v1/3_task_description_fig.png)

Figure 2: Antibody optimization task.

In this section, we present MemIG (Memory as Indexable Graphs), an
indexable, quantitative, and structured memory system for antibody
optimization agents. In this work, we consider the following formulation
of antibody optimization: given an antibody sequence, the model proposes
a set of mutations to improve a defined set of properties under a
maximum edit distance, as described in
[Figure 2](#S2.F2 "In 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

Throughout this section, an observation is a single measured effect of
applying mutations, and an insight is the summary of the observations
sharing the same identifier. Memory is then the graph whose nodes are
these insights and whose edges store how mutations interact when applied
together, as illustrated in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
Memory is self-evolving as the agent writes observations from its own
evaluations, constructs memory from the observations, and retrieves the
relevant insights.

Each component of MemIG realizes three properties of memory:
indexability, quantitativeness, and structured dependencies.
[Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Antibody-grounded insight identifier ‣ 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
defines the indexable identifiers and quantitative records,
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Epistasis graph ‣ 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
describes the epistasis graph, and
[Section 2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Memory retrieval ‣ 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
explains retrieval based on the constructed epistasis memory graph.

### 2.1 Antibody-grounded insight identifier

#### Indexable identifier.

The identifier makes memory indexable by addressing each insight with
the antibody context where it was observed. In detail, an identifier is
composed of a property, germline, region and mutation, where the region
is a contiguous block of residues that define a framework or
complementarity-determining region (e.g. FR1 or CDR2) and the mutation
position comes from AHo alignment  ([Honegger & PluÈckthun,
2001](#bib.bib11)), such as immunogenicity/IGHV3-23/\[cdr1\]/H:A47D. The
AHo scheme enables a single insight to accumulate evidence across
antibodies of different lengths. We use exact matching so that
observations are aggregated only when their biological context and
substitution match. Consequently, the same mutation observed under a
different context forms a different insight. This design is inspired by
[Zhang et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib29), which introduces identifiers to
enable local memory updates.

Addressing insights in this way keeps the memory update local and
efficient. Each new observation updates only the insight sharing its
identifier, leaving the rest of memory untouched. Therefore, the cost
scales with the number of identifiers affected by the new observation
rather than the total memory size, whereas rewriting the entire memory
grows more expensive as experience accumulates.

#### Quantitative record.

Each insight records the quantitative effect of its mutation, so that
memory reports exact quantities rather than free-form impressions. In
detail, an insight accumulates the mean effect across turns on each
property computed by the oracle, the number of observations, and the
directional votes over every observation sharing the identifier. The
directional vote records whether the mutation moved the property toward
the objective, so that the insight reports not only the average
magnitude of an effect but also how consistently that effect occurs. For
example, the insight

immunogenicity/IGHV3-23/H:A47D \[cdr1\]: avg -2.68, n=176,
$`\uparrow`$152/$`\downarrow`$24

records the substitution of alanine (A) with aspartate (D) at
heavy-chain position 47 in the CDR1 of a sequence from the IGHV3-23 gene
family. The mutation decreased (improved) immunogenicity by 2.68 on
average over 176 observations, and did so in all but 24 of them.

### 2.2 Epistasis graph

The epistasis graph makes memory structured by connecting insights whose
mutations interact. The joint effects of mutations may be non-additive
to other co-occurring mutations, a phenomenon known as epistasis, so a
set of independent insights cannot represent it. To capture this in the
epistasis graph, each node is a single mutation, and each edge
accumulates the joint effect of a co-occurring pair. These edges connect
mutations within a chain and across the heavy and light chains.

We measure the epistatic effect of a pair by decomposing each mutation
set the agent proposes. For each pair of mutations $`a`$ and $`b`$ in
the set, we additionally apply $`a`$ alone, $`b`$ alone, and $`a`$ and
$`b`$ together to the starting sequence, and measure the resulting
property changes $`\Delta_{a}`$, $`\Delta_{b}`$, and $`\Delta_{ab}`$.
Each node stores the mean isolated effect when the mutation is applied
alone as single_avg, while avg stores the mean effect of the complete
evaluated mutation sets containing that mutation to reflect the effects
of co-applied mutations.

![Refer to caption](2610.41245v1/2_memory_retrieve.png)

Figure 3: Memory retrieval of MemIG. Given a starting antibody, MemIG
identifies the matching identifiers, retrieves the corresponding
insights with their neighbors, and curates them into natural language.
Blue denotes the antibody-grounded identifier and the corresponding
node, green its quantitative record, and yellow the epistasis graph
neighbors and the curation based on them.

The epistatic effect is then the deviation of the pair from additivity,
$`\varepsilon_{ab}=\Delta_{ab}-\Delta_{a}-\Delta_{b}`$. When
$`\varepsilon_{ab}=0`$, the joint effect equals the sum of the
individual effects, indicating additivity and no epistasis. A nonzero
$`\varepsilon_{ab}`$ indicates an epistatic interaction: positive values
mean that the joint property change exceeds the sum of the individual
changes, whereas negative values mean that it falls below this sum. The
edge between $`a`$ and $`b`$ stores the mean of $`\Delta_{ab}`$ as
co*avg and the mean of $`\varepsilon*{ab}`$ as epistasis_avg over every
observation of that pair. Notably, this decomposition requires
additional oracle calls, which is possible because property oracles are
cheap and re-runnable on any sequence. An example of the stored nodes
and edges with these values is shown in
[Figure 3](#S2.F3 "In 2.2 Epistasis graph ‣ 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

### 2.3 Memory retrieval

Based on the constructed graph, memory is retrieved before each rollout
and injected into the prompt. The retrieval process consists of four
steps: identifier identification, ranking and selection, insight
retrieval, and insight curation, as described in
[Figure 3](#S2.F3 "In 2.2 Epistasis graph ‣ 2 Method: MemIG ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
In detail, we collect the insights whose identifiers match the germline
and the target properties of the current sequence, and whose mutations
match its wild-type residues at the corresponding AHo positions. We rank
them by their net directional votes breaking ties by the magnitude of
the avg, and select up to $`K`$ insights. In addition to these
exact-match insights, the memory also includes global insights that
aggregate mutation trends across germlines to capture broader mutation
trends, as detailed in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

The retrieved insights are curated into natural language so that the
agent receives interpretable guidance. Specifically, we curate each
insight with an LLM, which also receives up to $`N`$ 1-hop neighbor
insights and their edges from the epistasis graph, so that the text
describes both the isolated and joint effects. Curation produces the
guidance presented to the agent without modifying the stored
quantitative statistics. For example, an insight
immunogenicity/IGHV3-23/H:A47D \[cdr1\] is curated as:

immunogenicity/IGHV3-23/H:A47D \[cdr1\]: avg -2.68, n=176,
$`\uparrow`$152/$`\downarrow`$24; H:A47D (authoritative region: cdr1)
replaces a small nonpolar alanine with a negatively charged aspartate, a
charge-introduction change; its isolated effect is mild (single_avg
-0.114), so the -2.68 average (n=176) is mostly confounded by companion
mutations. Co-occurrence with other charge-introducing cdr2 mutations is
antagonistic — H:S59D (epistasis_avg +0.304) and H:L52S (+0.314) — while
H:K108D, H:Y70S, and fr3’s H:L12E are additive (0.0, -0.049, 0.0).

After curation, the curated insights are concatenated to form the memory
prompt. Memory is initialized as empty and the memory of the sequence is
written only after all of its rollouts have been scored. Therefore, the
rollouts of a sequence share the same memory snapshot, and a sequence
retrieves only the insights accumulated from the sequences optimized
before it. We provide an example of the constructed memory in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Examples ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

## 3 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate MemIG’s effectiveness on two antibody
optimization tasks. We employ Haiku-4.5 ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib2))
and GLM-5.3-Flash ([GLM-5-Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) as our backbone
models. We provide the detailed experimental settings in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

#### Metrics.

We employ two metrics throughout the experiments: pass@$`k`$ ([Chen
et al., 2021](#bib.bib3)) and improvement (Imp.). Here, we consider two
types of objectives: (1) minimization and maximization, which move the
property as far as possible in one direction, and (2) range, which moves
the property into a target interval. Pass@$`k`$ estimates the
probability that at least one of $`k`$ sampled rollouts passes, computed
as $`1-\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}`$, where $`n`$ rollouts are sampled
and $`c`$ pass. We report $`k\in\{1,3\}`$. A rollout passes when the
optimized sequence improves upon the starting sequence for minimization
and maximization tasks, or lies within the target interval for range
tasks.

Next, improvement measures the magnitude of the gain. Specifically, it
is computed as the signed difference between the optimized and the
starting property values in the favorable direction for minimization and
maximization tasks, and as the reduction in distance to the target
interval for range tasks. For example, in the range task, when the
starting sequence property is $`-0.6`$, and the optimized sequence
property is $`-0.4`$, the distance to the target interval
$`[-0.5,-0.2]`$ decreases from $`0.1`$ to $`0.0`$, giving an improvement
of $`0.1`$. Notably, both metrics are computed at the best turn of each
rollout determined by the reward and are then averaged over all
rollouts.

#### Baselines.

We utilize six baselines, including two statistical and four LLM-based
approaches. The statistical baselines include random and
MCMC ([Metropolis et al., 1953](#bib.bib16)). The random baseline
samples $`k`$ mutations uniformly from $`\{1,\dots,B\}`$ mutations,
where $`B`$ is the edit distance budget, and applies the mutations to
the starting variable fragment (Fv). The MCMC baseline runs
Metropolis-Hastings from the starting Fv. At each of $`T`$ steps,
matched to the turn budget of the agent, it proposes three random
mutations that remain within the edit distance budget, scores them with
the same reward $`r`$ used to evaluate the agent, and accepts the
mutations under the Metropolis criterion $`\min(1,\exp(\Delta r/\tau))`$
with the temperature fixed at $`\tau=1.0`$.

The LLM-based baselines include a vanilla LLM agent and three LLM agents
with different memory frameworks, including observations-only,
DC-Cu ([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), and ACE ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib29)). The vanilla LLM agent applies the agentic system
without memory. Next, the LLM agent with observations receives the same
oracle outputs that MemIG uses to construct its memory, but in their raw
form rather than aggregated under identifiers or curated. Lastly, DC-Cu
and ACE are self-evolving memory baselines that accumulate experience
across rollouts, where DC-Cu regenerates a compact cheatsheet after each
query while ACE maintains an indexed playbook updated through
incremental deltas. For fair comparison, we provide all LLM-based
baselines with the same tool access, prompt, maximum input and output
tokens, and turn budget, which isolates the contribution of the memory.

### 3.1 Multiple property optimization

#### Task description.

The goal of multiple property optimization is to satisfy multiple
property constraints at once by mutating the variable fragment (Fv) of a
given antibody sequence. Specifically, we select four antibody
properties: immunogenicity ([Thrift et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)),
liability count ([Cock et al., 2009](#bib.bib5)), GRAVY ([Kyte &
Doolittle, 1982](#bib.bib12)), and charge. Here, immunogenicity
quantifies the risk that the antibody triggers an unwanted immune
response and liability count measures chemically unstable sequence
motifs (e.g., oxidation and deamidation sites). Next, GRAVY measures the
average hydrophobicity over the residues and charge measures the net
charge of the sequence at pH 5.5. Immunogenicity and liability count are
minimization, and GRAVY and charge are range tasks, targeting
$`[-0.5,-0.2]`$ and $`[0.0,8.0]`$, respectively. We provide the details
in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

We randomly select 100 antibody sequences from the OAS dataset ([Olsen
et al., 2022](#bib.bib18)) and generate 10 rollouts per sequence. We
filter out the sequences that already satisfy the target constraint, so
the pass@$`k`$ of the starting sequences is zero by construction.

![Refer to caption](2610.41245v1/3_2_multiprop.png)

Figure 4: Multi property optimization results. Pass@1 and pass@3 (left)
and the distribution of improvement over the starting sequence (right),
where each colored dot is one rollout and the black diamond marks the
mean.

#### Results.

We provide the results in
[Figure 4](#S3.F4 "In Task description. ‣ 3.1 Multiple property optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
and full values in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
We observe that MemIG consistently improves multiple property
optimization across both backbones. Specifically, it achieves the
highest average improvement on Haiku-4.5 (0.718 vs. 0.602 for the
strongest baseline) and GLM-5.3-Flash (1.754 vs. 1.621), while also
attaining the best pass@1 on both backbones. The box plots show a broad
upward shift in the improvement, with medians close to the corresponding
means, indicating that the gains are systematic rather than driven by a
few favorable rollouts. Across all baseline comparisons, these gains are
significant under one-sided Mann–Whitney U tests ([Mann & Whitney,
1947](#bib.bib15)) with Holm–Bonferroni correction ($`p<0.005`$).

### 3.2 In silico antibody binding optimization

#### Task description.

The goal of this task is to optimize the binding of an antibody to a
given antigen by mutating CDR-H3. Specifically, we optimize two
confidence scores of a structure prediction model, the predicted TM
score (pTM) for the antibody structure and the interface predicted TM
score (AbAg-ipTM) for the antibody-antigen interaction, where we target
$`>0.8`$ and $`>0.7`$ respectively. Such confidence scores discriminate
binders from non-binders and therefore serve as useful proxies for in
silico binding optimization ([Abramson et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Lin
et al., 2022](#bib.bib13); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib30)). We employ
Protenix-v2 ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib30)) for its predictive power
and open availability.

We select antibody-antigen complexes from the SAbDab  ([Dunbar et al.,
2014](#bib.bib8)). We retain only complexes that are (i) of type
fragment antigen-binding (Fab), (ii) bound to a single antigen chain,
and (iii) whose CDR-H3 loop makes substantial contact with the antigen
interface (H3 interface fraction $`>0.3`$). These selected complexes are
grouped into $`11`$ clusters, where each cluster is treated as one
optimization task, generating 30 rollouts per complex. We provide the
details includng the number of complexes and their PDB IDs in each
cluster in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

Figure 5: In silico antibody binding optimization. Each numeric label
corresponds to an antibody-antigen cluster, clustered by CDR sequence
identity. ^(∗) denotes the structural baselines (dashed), which have
access to the complex structure.

#### Baselines.

We add two structural baselines for in silico antibody optimization
task, including ProteinMPNN ([Dauparas et al., 2022](#bib.bib6)) and
AbMPNN ([Dreyer et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)). These baselines inverse-fold
the native complex with every position fixed except CDR-H3. It is
notable that they receive the backbone coordinates of the
antibody-antigen complex, whereas MemIG observes the sequence alone. We
sample the same number of designs as the agent’s turn budget and
evaluate all designs with the same oracle. We treat these methods as
structure-informed references because they receive complex backbone
coordinates, whereas MEMIG receives only sequences. They could also be
incorporated into the agent as design tools.

#### Results.

We provide the results in
[Figure 5](#S3.F5 "In Task description. ‣ 3.2 In silico antibody binding optimization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
and the detailed values in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
Among the non-structural methods, we observe that MemIG attains the best
pass@1 in 9 of the 11 clusters with GLM-5.3-Flash and in 7 of the 11
clusters with Haiku-4.5, and the highest improvement in every cluster
with GLM- 5.3-Flash. Compared to all LLM-based and statistical baselines
within each backbone, these gains are statistically significant under
one-sided Mann–Whitney U tests ([Mann & Whitney, 1947](#bib.bib15)) with
Holm–Bonferroni correction ($`p<0.005`$). The structural baselines
included as reference anchors lead on improvement, since improvement is
averaged over all designs regardless of whether they pass the
constraint. Notably, ProteinMPNN attains a pass rate of zero in 8 of the
11 clusters while leading on improvement in three of them, which shows
that a large improvement does not imply that the designs reach the
target.

### 3.3 Analysis

We conduct the following analyses on the in silico antibody binding
optimization task with GLM-5.3-Flash on three randomly picked clusters
(148, 193, 993). We provide additional analyses including same oracle
call analysis and details in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

| Component    | Pass@1 | Pass@3 | Imp.  |
| ------------ | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| MemIG (Ours) | 0.149  | 0.278  | 0.125 |
| Identifier   | 0.074  | 0.153  | 0.117 |
| Epistasis    | 0.049  | 0.130  | 0.142 |
| Vanilla LLM  | 0.015  | 0.047  | 0.067 |

Table 1: Ablation study on component.

#### Ablation study on component.

We ablate the components of MemIG. In detail, the indexable identifier
drops the germline+region field which keeps property and mutation only.
Next, the epistasis graph removes the edges, so that memory stores the
information of each mutation without access to the joint effects. As
shown in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.3 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization"),
we observe that every ablation degrades the pass rate, which shows that
all components contribute to satisfying the constraints. In contrast,
the ablated epistasis attain a higher improvement, since improvement is
averaged over all designs regardless of whether they satisfy the
constraint.

#### Memory faithfulness.

We next verify that the agent actually uses the retrieved insights
stored in memory by MemIG. In detail, we take the insights that MemIG
retrieves for each starting antibody as a fixed reference set, and
compare MEMIG’s proposals with this reference set. The adoption measures
the fraction of proposed mutations that appear anywhere in the reference
set, while helpful and harmful adoption further split this fraction by
whether the recorded effect of the matched insight points toward or
against the objective based on their directional votes. Since a mutation
has a separate insight for each property, it can be helpful for one and
harmful for another, so the two fractions sum to more than the total
adoption. Additionally, we report the net directional alignment, a gap
between helpful and harmful adoption ($`\Delta`$), as the agent must not
only read the memory but also distinguish its direction.

| Adoption | Helpful | Harmful | $`\Delta`$ |
| -------- | ------- | ------- | ---------- |
| 0.931    | 0.909   | 0.004   | 0.905      |

Table 2: Memory faithfulness. MemIG raises both adoption and net
directional alignment.

We provide the results in
[Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Memory faithfulness. ‣ 3.3 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").
We observe that 93.1% of the proposals by MemIG were present in the
memory. These mutations were mostly from helpful insights, not from
harmful insights, which shows that the agent reads and understands the
recorded direction of an insight.

Figure 6: Cumulative performance progression. Vertical lines mark memory
updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently
under the same memory. The curves report the centered rolling mean with
a half-width of 30 rollouts, computed within each memory step. Notably,
the ordering of rollouts within the same memory is random, so a downward
slope does not imply performance decrease. Each dot marks the mean over
all rollouts of that memory step.

#### Cumulative performance progression.

We analyze how performance changes as memory self-evolves in
[Figure 6](#S3.F6 "In Memory faithfulness. ‣ 3.3 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
by tracking the improvement of the vanilla LLM and MemIG at each memory
step, where the rollouts sharing a memory step are generated
concurrently. We report clusters 148 and 993, whose germline remains
constant across the starting complexes, so that the insights accumulated
from earlier rollouts apply directly to later ones. We observe that
MemIG improves over memory versions while the vanilla LLM stays near
flat, so the gain comes from the accumulated memory rather than from the
agent itself. Notably, the gap widens after the first memory update and
remains positive, which shows that MemIG improves through
self-evolution. We additionally report the same analysis without the
rolling average in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

## 4 Related work

#### Self-evolving agent with memory.

Self-evolving agents have recently gained substantial attention, where
agents accumulate experience from past rollouts and store it into
external memory without updating model weights ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22)). ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) abstracts
natural language insights from successful and failed experience, and
maintains them through LLM-judged upvotes and downvotes. Dynamic
Cheatsheet ([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)) generates the solution
based on the current cheat sheet, curates the insight based on the
generation, and updates the cheat sheet, while ACE ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib29)) instead maintains an itemized playbook with helpful
and harmful counters, updated with incremental deltas.

Graph-based memories keep their entries as linked notes rather than a
flat list, where nodes and edges represent semantic relations between
textual memories ([Chhikara et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28)). Nevertheless, these approaches store experience as
natural language written and judged by an LLM, address entries by opaque
labels that do not encode applicability context, and connect entries by
textual relatedness. To address these challenges, MemIG stores
oracle-measured quantities under the biological context-derived
identifiers and connects them through oracle-measured interactions.

#### LLM agents for protein optimization.

Protein sequence optimization has been studied as black-box optimization
over a discrete space, where a model is trained on previously evaluated
sequences and is used to propose the next candidates ([Stanton et al.,
2022](#bib.bib23); [Gruver et al., 2023](#bib.bib10); [Notin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17)). Recently, LLM agents have entered this pipeline by
orchestrating property predictors as tools and reasoning over the
returned scores to select or revise candidates, with some accumulating
design strategies across rollouts as natural language ([Roohani et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Tan et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)). However, these approaches only accumulate narrative
feedback without any quantitative record, which is not indexed and not
structured in terms of biological context. To address this, MemIG keeps
oracle-measured effects under antibody-grounded insight identifiers and
connects them through measured pairwise interactions, which keeps
accumulated memory indexable, quantitative, and structured across
rollouts.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce MemIG, a memory construction framework for
antibody optimization agents that keeps accumulated observations
indexable, quantitative, and structured rather than narrated. Each
insight is addressed by an antibody-grounded identifier over the
property, germline, region, and mutation, and stores the effect measured
by a property oracle. Next, edges between insights record the epistatic
effect based on how mutations behave when applied together. Our findings
suggest that the unit of memory should be defined by the domain it
serves, and that grounding memory in measured quantities rather than
generated text allows experience to accumulate without summarization.
Although we instantiate MEMIG for antibody optimization, the framework
can extend to other oracle-guided optimization problems when the domain
provides a suitable identifier.

#### Limitation and challenge.

First, our evaluation is conducted in silico using computational
property oracles. This bounds the cost model of the epistasis
decomposition, which assumes oracles that can be re-run freely. Although
these oracles provide a controlled testbed, improvements may not
directly translate to experimentally measured properties. Second, MemIG
currently represents mutation interactions through pairwise epistasis
edges. Although each edge is estimated by evaluating the individual
mutations and their pair, multi-mutation designs may exhibit
higher-order interactions. Next, the curation step of MemIG relies on
the capability of the backbone model, as in prior work ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib29); [Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)). If the model
fails to describe a retrieved insight faithfully, the curated guidance
may be misleading while the quantitative record mitigates this.

## Ethics statement

This work studies memory construction for antibody optimization agents,
and the experiments are conducted in silico with computational property
oracles. We use only publicly released data, including antibody
sequences from OAS ([Olsen et al., 2022](#bib.bib18)) and
antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab ([Dunbar et al.,
2014](#bib.bib8)), under their respective licenses; the OAS sequences
derive from published immune repertoire studies and are not linked to
identifiable individuals, and no human subjects are involved in our
experiments. MemIG optimizes developability and predicted interface
confidence rather than any property related to toxicity or
pathogenicity, and any resulting candidate would require experimental
validation and human review before use.

## Reproducibility statement

We provide the information required to reproduce our experiments in the
main text and appendix.
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
describes the evaluation setup and baselines, while
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
provides the property oracles, datasets, prompts, and hyperparameters.
Complete numerical results and additional analyses are reported in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

## AI Disclosure

We used generative AI tools to polish writing of the manuscript, create
figures, and assist with analysis and plotting code. The research
hypothesis, the method design, and all experiments were determined by
the authors. The remaining tasks requiring disclosure, such as
generating synthetic datasets and writing proofs, are not applicable.

### B.1 Details of optimized properties

We provide the details of the optimized properties, including the oracle
and the description of their significance in
[Table A1](#A2.T1 "In B.1 Details of optimized properties ‣ Appendix B Experimental details ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization").

| Property       | Objective | Oracle                                            | Why it matters                                                                                |
| -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Immunogenicity | Minimize  | Pep2Vec  ([Thrift et al., 2024](#bib.bib27))      | Predicted MHC class II epitope cores that can provoke an anti-drug antibody response.         |
| Liabilities    | Minimize  | Biopython  ([Cock et al., 2009](#bib.bib5))       | Motifs that degrade during manufacture and storage, costing potency and shelf life.           |
| GRAVY          | Range     | Biopython  ([Kyte & Doolittle, 1982](#bib.bib12)) | Exposed hydrophobicity drives aggregation, but an overly hydrophilic domain loses stability.  |
| Charge         | Range     | Biopython  ([Cock et al., 2009](#bib.bib5))       | Endosomal charge at pH 5.5 governs clearance rate and formulation viscosity at both extremes. |
| pTM            | Range     | Protenix ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib30))      | Predicted TM-score between the predicted and the true complex.                                |
| AbAg iPTM      | Range     | Protenix ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib30))      | Accuracy of the predicted relative placement of the antibody and the antigen.                 |

Table A1: Optimized properties. Six antibody properties the agent
optimizes, the oracle or function measuring each, and why each are
significant.

Heavy and Light chain CDR loops are concatenated into one string.
Mmseqs2 ([Steinegger & Söding, 2017](#bib.bib24)) is run with a 70%
sequence identity cutoff.

### B.3 Details of global insight construction

Global insights capture mutation trends that are shared across germlines
in addition to the context-specific insights retrieved by exact
matching. In detail, we aggregate observations for each property by
their mutation target, such as to K, and record the mean property
effect, number of observations, and directional votes. These insights
are stored separately from the exact-match insights and are included in
the memory prompt together with the retrieved local insights. Global
insights provide broader evidence when a mutation trend transfers across
biological contexts. Notably, they complement rather than replace the
context-specific insights defined by the antibody-grounded identifier.

## Appendix C Additional experimental results

### C.1 Cumulative performance progression without a rolling average

Figure 7: Cumulative performance progression without a rolling average.
Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines
are generated concurrently under the same memory. Each point is the mean
improvement over all rollouts sharing a memory step, and error bars
indicate the standard error across those rollouts.

The rolling average in
[Figure 6](#S3.F6 "In Memory faithfulness. ‣ 3.3 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
smooths the rollouts within each memory step, which can obscure the
value of an individual step. To remove this smoothing, we report the
mean improvement of every rollout sharing a memory step as a single
point in
[Figure 7](#A3.F7 "In C.1 Cumulative performance progression without a rolling average ‣ Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization"),
with error bars indicating the standard error across those rollouts. We
observe the same trend as in
[Figure 6](#S3.F6 "In Memory faithfulness. ‣ 3.3 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization"),
where MemIG improves over successive memory steps while the vanilla LLM
does not, which confirms that the progression is not an artifact of the
smoothing.

### C.2 Same oracle call analysis

| Cluster | Model        | Pass@1 | Pass@3 | Avg   |
| ------- | ------------ | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| 148     | DC-Cu\*      | 0.067  | 0.182  | 0.109 |
|         | ACE\*        | 0.100  | 0.215  | 0.169 |
|         | MemIG (Ours) | 0.258  | 0.456  | 0.144 |
| 193     | DC-Cu\*      | 0.056  | 0.159  | 0.110 |
|         | ACE\*        | 0.028  | 0.081  | 0.107 |
|         | MemIG (Ours) | 0.194  | 0.374  | 0.141 |
| 993     | DC-Cu\*      | 0.000  | 0.000  | 0.070 |
|         | ACE\*        | 0.000  | 0.000  | 0.070 |
|         | MemIG (Ours) | 0.007  | 0.020  | 0.090 |

Table A4: Comparison under the same oracle calls. Bold highlights the
best score in a cluster and \* denotes additional decomposition oracle
call mode.

We compare MemIG against the memory baselines under a matched oracle
budget, since the decomposition of MemIG consumes additional oracle
calls. Here, single-mutation and pairwise decomposition is an epistasis
graph component of MemIG rather than a shared experimental setting,
since ACE ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib29)) and DC-Cu ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)) accumulate experience from the trajectories an agent
produces. Therefore, modifying them is not required for a fair
comparison, as the decomposition is part of what we propose rather than
an advantage granted by the setup. Nevertheless, we report a setting in
which ACE and DC-Cu receive the same decomposed measurements, which
removes any difference in the oracle call budget between the methods.

We provide the results in
[Table A4](#A3.T4 "In C.2 Same oracle call analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
under GLM-5.3-flash backbone. We observe that MemIG attains the highest
pass@1 and pass@3 on all three clusters even when the baselines share
the same oracle calls, which shows that the gain comes from how the
measurements are stored rather than from access to them. Here, ACE
attains a higher average improvement on one cluster while satisfying the
constraints less often, which is consistent with the observation that
improvement is averaged over all designs regardless of whether they
satisfy the constraint.

### C.3 Cost analysis

| Method      | Input | Output | Pass@1 | Tokens / pass |
| ----------- | ----- | ------ | ------ | ------------- |
| Vanilla LLM | 98.1  | 6.8    | 0.022  | 4.719M        |
| Obs.        | 204.3 | 7.2    | 0.000  | –             |
| ACE         | 103.8 | 6.6    | 0.017  | 6.623M        |
| DC-Cu       | 120.3 | 7.7    | 0.006  | 23.028M       |
| MemIG       | 270.1 | 9.2    | 0.194  | 1.436M        |

Table A5: Token cost analysis. Average token consumption per rollout.
Input and output tokens are reported in thousands. Tokens per pass
include tokens consumed by unsuccessful rollouts.

| Method      | Ref. | Candidate | Single | Pair  | Total |
| ----------- | ---- | --------- | ------ | ----- | ----- |
| Vanilla LLM | 1.00 | 6.03      | 0      | 0     | 07.03 |
| Obs.        | 1.00 | 5.88      | 0      | 0     | 06.88 |
| ACE         | 1.00 | 5.44      | 0      | 0     | 06.44 |
| DC-Cu       | 1.00 | 5.76      | 0      | 0     | 06.76 |
| MemIG       | 1.00 | 4.95      | 8.46   | 22.97 | 37.38 |

Table A6: Oracle evaluation cost. Average number of oracle evaluations
per rollout. Single and pair evaluations are additional evaluations used
by MemIG to construct the epistasis graph.

We report the computational cost of GLM-5.3-Flash on the in silico
antibody binding optimization task (cluster 193). As shown in
[Table A5](#A3.T5 "In C.3 Cost analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization"),
MemIG uses more input tokens because the retrieved memory is injected
before each rollout, while achieving the highest Pass@1 and the lowest
token cost per successful rollout. While the absolute token usage is
highest, the token cost per successful rollout reduces to 1.436M,
compared with $`>`$4M for all baselines.

[Table A6](#A3.T6 "In C.3 Cost analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional experimental results ‣ MemIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization")
reports the mean number of unique oracle inputs per rollout. The
additional single- and pair-mutation inputs introduced by MemIG’s
epistasis decomposition increase this for $`\binom{n}{2}+n`$ where n
denotes the number of proposed mutations. This increase is by design, as
MemIG explicitly evaluates isolated mutations and pairs to measure
epistasis, and these additional evaluations remain practical in our in
silico setting because the computational oracles are easily re-runnable
without experimental measurements. Moreover, the decomposition budget is
a tunable knob rather than a structural requirement. For example, pairs
can be subsampled instead of exhaustively decomposed, so the design does
not depend on oracles being free.
